sections.title: Whose is it? Put it on the noun
sections.content: You already know *-m* ('my') and *-d* ('your') from the family words (*anyám*, *anyád*). Now add the third person, 'his' or 'her': *-a / -e* or *-ja / -je*. Hungarian has no separate little word for 'his' or 'her'. The ending on the noun does the job, so *kulcsa* means both 'his key' and 'her key'. Who the owner is comes from the situation: *Anna itt van. A kulcsa ott van.* (Anna is here. Her key is there.)

sections.title: One owner, three persons
rows: my key, your key, his/her key
my book, your book, his/her book
my phone, your phone, his/her phone
my bag, your bag, his/her bag

sections.title: Which 3rd-person ending?
sections.content:
Look at the last letter of the noun. After a vowel the ending is *-ja / -je*, and a final *a* or *e* lengthens to *á* or *é*: *táska* → *táskám*, *táskád*, *táskája*. (*anya* and *apa* are irregular in the 3rd person: *anyja*, *apja*, not *anyája*, *apája*.) After a consonant the ending is *-a / -e* or *-ja / -je*, and the word decides: *kulcsa* and *könyve*, but *telefonja*. Back-vowel words take *-a / -ja* and front-vowel words take *-e / -je*. Learn the form together with the word.

Linking vowel: after a consonant, *-m* and *-d* need a vowel in front of them: *kulcs* → *kulcsom*, *kulcsod*; *könyv* → *könyvem*, *könyved*. The 3rd person needs no linking vowel, because *-a / -e* is already a vowel: *kulcsa*, *könyve*.

items.spanish: Anna itt van. A táskája nagy.
items.english: Anna is here. Her bag is big.

sections.content: English makes you choose between 'his' and 'her' and puts a separate word in front. Hungarian does neither: *a kulcsa* is 'his key' or 'her key', and the ending is all you add. Keep the endings apart: *a telefonom* is my phone, *a telefonja* is his or hers.
